sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Ever felt like `if-else` chains are getting too messy? Let’s learn a cleaner way to handle multiple choices!

• How `switch` statements simplify multi-way branching
• When to use `switch` vs `if-else`
• The magic of `break` and `default` cases

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
📊 Visual Simulation
sections.content: Step-by-step visualization of how `switch` statements work:

steps.title: 🔍 Case Matching
steps.description: It jumps to the matching case (like a teleporter!).

steps.title: ⏹️ Break or Fall Through
steps.description: `break` exits the switch. Without it, code ‘falls through’ to the next case!

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ `switch` is cleaner than long `if-else` chains for multiple conditions
✓ Always include `break` unless you want ‘fall-through’ behavior
✓ `default` case handles unexpected values (like a safety net)
✓ Cases must be constant values (no variables!)

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Use `switch` for 3+ conditions to keep code readable
Group cases without `break` for shared logic (e.g., weekdays)
donts: Use non-constant cases (e.g., `case x:` where `x` is a variable)
sections.protip: For complex conditions, combine `switch` with enums for type safety!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where is `switch` used in real apps?

examples.how: Handling user input (e.g., ‘Press 1 for Settings’) in CLI apps.

problem.description:
Write a `switch` statement that converts a month number (1-12) to its name. Handle invalid numbers with `default`.
Example: Input `3` → Output `"March"`.
problem.explanation: Each `case` maps a number to its month name. The `default` catches invalid inputs (e.g., 13). Without `break`, the code would print all months after the match!

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 `switch` simplifies multi-way branching with clean syntax
📌 Practice with real-world menus or game controls
📌 Ready to combine with loops next!
